title: Can oil deals reset US-Iraqi relations?
gist: As US troops leave Iraq by September 30, PM Ali al-Zaidi is trying to replace security ties with oil deals (headline $60-200 billion), bring back ExxonMobil and Chevron, and build Basra-Haditha and Syria/Turkey export pipelines after Hormuz closure cut over 90% of Iraqi exports, but militias, contract terms and a short Trump window are the key risks.

insights.claim: The Hormuz closure has cut off more than 90% of Iraqi oil exports, and Iraq's domestic pipeline system can move under 250,000 b/d south-to-north to Turkey via the Iraq-Turkey Pipeline.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Iraqi supply is largely offline while Hormuz is shut — a major driver of global crude tightness.
insights.locator: For Baghdad, the strategic necessity is evident.

insights.claim: The conflict has already cost Iraq at least $40 billion in potential oil export revenue.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Fiscal strain for a state where oil is 90%+ of revenue — risk to Iraqi public payrolls and stability.
insights.locator: The oil ministry has brought in US services firm KBR

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia shut its east-west oil pipeline after drones launched from Iraq severely damaged it.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Even Hormuz-bypass routes are vulnerable — raises risk premium on Gulf supply alternatives.

insights.claim: Iraq has trucked fuel oil to Syria's Baniyas terminal since early April as a test case for a proposed two million b/d Iraq-Syria export pipeline.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Syria emerging as a Mediterranean export hub for Middle East energy.
insights.locator: Facing the collapse of exports through the Gulf

insights.claim: Zaidi's July White House visit produced preliminary deals initially pegged at over $60 billion, mostly oil, later inflated to $200 billion, as Trump framed US oil companies replacing withdrawing US forces.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Headline deal values are inflated; treat as optionality rather than committed capex.

insights.claim: Iraq targets raising production capacity from five million b/d to seven million b/d by 2030, with US company entry central to the plan.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Potential +2 mb/d of supply by 2030 — bearish long-run supply factor if delivered.
insights.locator: The entry of US companies is also central

insights.claim: Western majors exited Iraq mainly for commercial reasons — low-margin technical service contracts, centralized management and payment delays — rather than security: Statoil/Equinor in 2012, Occidental 2016, Shell 2018, ExxonMobil 2024; Chinese firms filled the gap.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Contract terms, not security, are the gating factor for Western capex in Iraq.
insights.quote: These commercial challenges, more than the security risks in southern Iraq, prompted several leading companies to withdraw.

insights.claim: Iraq's 2018 profit-sharing contracts marked a turning point, enabling TotalEnergies' $27 billion Gas Growth Integrated Project in Basra in 2023 and BP's award of the Kirkuk redevelopment in 2025.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Improved fiscal terms make Iraq investable again for majors.
insights.locator: The oil ministry began changing course

insights.claim: Iraq seeks ExxonMobil for the 450,000 b/d Majnoon field and Chevron for the 480,000 b/d West Qurna-2 field, from which Lukoil was ousted after US sanctions; preliminary terms with Chevron are under way, with progress with HKN and Halliburton.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Upstream growth optionality for XOM and CVX in Iraq; Lukoil loses a flagship asset.

insights.claim: If Exxon, Chevron and other US projects proceed, US firms could operate at least 1.5 million b/d of Iraqi production, surpassing Chinese-operated capacity; BP has already brought ConocoPhillips into Kirkuk.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Shift of Iraqi operatorship from Chinese to US firms — non-US operators seek US partners.

insights.claim: Baghdad signed with a Qatari-US consortium including Chevron to study pipelines from Haditha west to Baniyas and north to Ceyhan, underpinned by the 2.25 million b/d, $4.6 billion Basra-Haditha pipeline; KBR is consultant and total new pipelines are expected to cost at least $15 billion.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Contract flow for pipeline EPC and oil services firms such as KBR.
insights.locator: Baghdad has signed a deal with a Qatari-US consortium

insights.claim: The Basra-Haditha pipeline and related facilities could take up to four years, excluding cross-border extensions, and Syria's pipeline network must be built from scratch after fourteen years of civil war.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: No near-term relief for Iraqi exports from new pipelines — Hormuz status remains the dominant driver.
insights.locator: But the Iraqi government must act quickly

insights.claim: ConocoPhillips is considering developing the Akkas gas field in Anbar, with potential synergies with its Syrian gas assets, as smaller US operators in Iraqi Kurdistan expand into northeast Syria.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Cross-border Iraq-Syria gas plays emerging for US E&Ps.

insights.claim: Turkey unilaterally exited the 1973 ITP treaty last year and imposed a harsh interim one-year deal ending Iraq's exclusive access and raising transit fees; a Syrian outlet would strengthen Iraq's negotiating hand.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Watch ITP renewal terms; Syrian route diversification reduces Turkish leverage.
insights.locator: A Syrian outlet would also strengthen

insights.claim: Alternative export corridors that reduce Iran's Hormuz leverage will likely garner bipartisan US support and outlast the Trump presidency.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Bypass infrastructure is a multi-administration theme, lowering US policy risk for these projects.

insights.claim: Zaidi's window is narrow: a Democrat-controlled Congress from January could scrutinize Middle East dealmaking, and Trump leaves office in 2029.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Deal momentum may stall after midterms — execution risk for announced Iraqi contracts.
insights.locator: The window to engage the Trump White House

insights.claim: Iran-backed militias using Iraqi territory to attack Gulf states, Kurdistan and US interests have prompted US strikes, temporary restrictions on dollar transfers and sanctions on a senior Iraqi oil official.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US dollar-access and sanctions tools are live risks for Iraqi banks and oil flows.

insights.claim: Without militia disarmament, any expanded US commercial presence in Iraq's oil sector would be exposed to attacks, giving militias a new way to pressure both Baghdad and Washington.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Security is the key test for US majors' Iraq investments — monitor disarmament progress.
insights.quote: The most important test is security.
insights.locator: The most important test is security.

insights.claim: Oil revenues exceed 90% of Iraqi state income, but the sector competes for funding with rising public salaries and welfare spending, historically narrowing capital for upstream projects.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Fiscal crowding-out raises reliance on foreign capital and IOC-friendly terms.
